meta.title: Punctuation Power: Combining Sentences for Effect

questions.prompt: Combine the two sentences so the second event feels sudden and dramatic: "The bell rang. The students hurried to class."
choices: The bell rang: the students hurried to class.
The bell rang— the students hurried to class.
The bell rang; the students hurried to class.
The bell rang, the students hurried to class.
questions.explanation: The dash creates an abrupt, dramatic shift that emphasizes the suddenness of the students' reaction.
questions.topic: Combine Two Sentences - Punctuation for Effect

questions.prompt: Combine the two sentences to convey an abrupt, dramatic shift: "The candle flickered. Shadows stretched across the wall."
choices: The candle flickered; shadows stretched across the wall.
The candle flickered: shadows stretched across the wall.
The candle flickered— shadows stretched across the wall.
The candle flickered, shadows stretched across the wall.
questions.explanation: A dash creates a sudden, dramatic break that makes the second clause feel like an immediate, striking shift.
questions.topic: Combine Two Sentences - Punctuation for Effect

questions.prompt: Combine the two sentences to show two related but independent outcomes of equal weight: "The phone rang. No one answered."
choices: The phone rang, no one answered.
The phone rang: no one answered.
The phone rang— no one answered.
The phone rang; no one answered.
questions.explanation: A semicolon joins two independent clauses that are closely related yet remain separate statements of equal importance.
questions.topic: Combine Two Sentences - Punctuation for Effect
